    Glossary

    This glossary collects terms used throughout the training, with the definitions given where each term is introduced.

    Ontology
    A formal, explicit specification of a shared conceptualisation. See Introduction to ontologies.
    Conceptualisation
    A model of the things and relationships relevant to a domain, or area of interest.
    RDF (Resource Description Framework)
    A W3C standard data model that expresses descriptions and links as statements (triples) about resources. See Linked Data Foundations.
    Triple
    A single RDF statement with a subject (what is described), a predicate (the property or relationship), and an object (what it relates to, or a value).
    IRI (Internationalized Resource Identifier)
    A name used in RDF to identify a resource consistently across datasets.
    Linked Data
    An approach to publishing structured data on the Web, using Web identifiers, HTTP(S) lookups, RDF descriptions and links to other identifiers, so that related information can be found by following links.
    Knowledge graph
    A representation of things and their relationships in a graph data model; this course covers knowledge graphs that use RDF and follow Linked Data principles.
    Class
    In OWL, a kind of thing, such as Bicycle or Frame.
    Individual
    In OWL, a particular thing; an instance of a class, such as B001 as an instance of Bicycle.
    Object property
    A property that represents a relationship between individuals, such as “has component”.
    Datatype property
    A property that links an individual to a data value, such as “has material”.
    Literal
    A data value in the object position of an RDF triple, with a datatype that tells applications how to interpret its written value.
    OWL (Web Ontology Language)
    A W3C standard, built on RDF, for representing ontologies on the Web so that applications can exchange and reason over them. See Logical modelling in OWL.
    Reasoner
    Software that uses OWL reasoning to check consistency and class satisfiability and to infer additional statements from an ontology and its data, such as HermiT.
    Open-world assumption (OWA)
    The assumption, made by OWL, that a statement can be true even when it has not been recorded or inferred; absence of a statement does not mean it is false.
    Axiom
    A statement that an ontology asserts to hold, such as a subclass statement or a class equivalence.
    Restriction
    A class expression that describes individuals through a property, such as hasComponent some Frame.
    Entailment
    A statement that follows logically in every model of an ontology and its data.
    Consistency
    A property of an ontology meaning that at least one model exists in which all its axioms hold together.
    Class satisfiability
    The property that a class can have a member in some model, even in a consistent ontology.
    SPARQL
    A query language for RDF data, used to match patterns of statements and retrieve the information they contain. See Linked Data Foundations.
    SHACL (Shapes Constraint Language)
    A W3C standard for validating RDF graphs against chosen requirements, expressed as shapes.
    Triple store
    A database for storing and querying RDF, often exposing a SPARQL endpoint.
    Competency question
    A question that an ontology, together with relevant data, should help answer; used to scope and check the coverage of a model. See Design your own ontology.
    IRI strategy
    A consistent pattern for creating ontology, term and individual identifiers, including a maintainable Web domain and HTTPS.

    W3C standards and guides

    The training uses RDF 1.1, OWL 2 and SPARQL 1.1. Start with the primers; consult the specifications for definitions and details.

    Primers and guides

    OWL 2 Primer An introduction to OWL with examples
    OWL 2 Document Overview A guide to the OWL specifications
    OWL 2 Quick Reference A summary of OWL constructs
    OWL 2 Manchester Syntax Readable OWL syntax used in Protégé
    SKOS Primer Concept schemes, labels and mappings
    SPARQL 1.1 Overview A guide to queries, updates, protocols and result formats

    Optional guidance on ontology development

    • Ontology Development 101 (2001): process guidance on scope, reuse and iterative modelling. Its examples use older tools; this course uses OWL 2.
    • OBO Academy: community training on OWL and ontology curation, with a biological and biomedical focus. Its SubClassOf versus EquivalentTo explanation uses diagrams to compare the two axioms.

    Related work

    Books

    • Semantic Web for the Working Ontologist (Allemang and Hendler, 2nd ed., 2011): worked examples of modelling with RDF, RDFS and OWL, and querying with SPARQL.
    • An Introduction to Ontology Engineering (Keet, 2nd ed., 2025): a more technical treatment of formal foundations and ontology development methods. The author’s site also provides an earlier open edition.

    Ontology development methodologies

    • METHONTOLOGY (Fernández-López et al., 1997): a lifecycle approach using evolving prototypes, with evaluation and documentation throughout development.
    • NeOn (Suárez-Figueroa et al., 2012): guidance for different development scenarios, particularly reusing and combining existing knowledge resources.
    • LOT (Linked Open Terms) (Poveda-Villalón et al., 2022): an iterative workflow covering requirements, implementation, publication and maintenance, with practical guidance and workflow diagrams.
